extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (authors wanting to write believable gendered dialogue), especially speculative fiction and YA writers
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and criteria for writing authentic, character-serving gendered dialogue: how to use Genderlect theory, group dynamics, socialization, and research to craft voices that convey relationship, status, and background without heavy exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Genderlect theory as a heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Genderlect theory (Deborah Tannen): women, in general, seek connections while men seek status; this influences style and language choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat this as a broad-brush heuristic, not a rule that applies to every individual. Use the insight that motivations differ (connection vs status) to inform how characters phrase things and what they're trying to accomplish in conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapport talk vs report talk
rubrics_metrics.description: Women use rapport talk (building bonds, compliments); men use report talk (establishing status, joking insults).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the difference to stage group openings: e.g., a woman joining women might receive a compliment; a man joining men might get joking razzing. Use these patterns to show group dynamics and relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model group dynamics to reveal relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Group-first-comments and exchange patterns (compliments among women; joking insults among men) establish dominance, belonging, and relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage first comments, teasing, self-deprecation, and reciprocal giving of compliments or insults to show who belongs, who leads, and the hierarchy in a group. Making a character conform or not conform to group norms can signal charisma or outsider status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show motivations through dialogue (goal-oriented vs bond-building)
rubrics_metrics.description: Men tend to be goal-oriented (try to 'fix' problems); women tend to seek empathy and emotional connection when recounting events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have characters respond in ways that reflect those motives: offer solutions vs offer empathy. Use interruptions, offers to solve, or lending sympathy to demonstrate differing conversational priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for socialization and the spectrum of behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Most gendered differences are the result of socialization; there's a broad spectrum and many exceptions (including neuroatypicality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid stereotyping by acknowledging variation—exceptions are as interesting as the rules and can create richer characters. Use socialization as an explanatory layer, not a straightjacket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make dialogue serve story and character
rubrics_metrics.description: Write dialog which serves our stories and our characters, communicating background and relationships without explicit exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let speech patterns, choices, and interactions implicitly convey upbringing, class, region, and role. Avoid telling the reader where a character is from; show it through how they speak and what they prioritize in conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity: read material written by and for that gender
rubrics_metrics.description: To learn the other side, read work written by and for that gender (e.g., romance and women's magazines for women; men's magazines/urban survivalist material for men).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consume genre-specific and audience-specific material to internalize rhythms and idioms. This is practical immersion: read widely in the target voice to capture authentic patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get target-gender readers to flag issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Have someone of the gender you're writing read and flag dialogue that feels wrong or inauthentic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use beta readers specifically to identify mismatches (e.g., dialogue that is too complimentary, not sufficiently razzing, or uses the wrong kinds of equivocation). Incorporate feedback and iterate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use listening/observation research (but ethically)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spend more time listening than you spend talking; observe conversations in public (coffee shops, etc.) to learn real speech patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listen to how people actually talk to pick up rhythms and interactions, but avoid inappropriate or predatory behavior (explicit caution against 'hanging around' vulnerable groups like teenage girls).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flag and edit equivocating language (apologies, hedges, self-deprecation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Women often apologize, are overly polite, use equivocating language and self-deprecation; these traits can be characteristic but also overused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tools (e.g., the Gmail plugin 'Just Not Sorry') or manual editing to identify hedges and unnecessary apologies. Decide intentionally how much equivocating a character should have—too much becomes annoying or one-note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use self-deprecation and razzing appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Women may razz themselves; men razz others—both are social tools to build or policed bonds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance self-deprecation so characters aren't constantly undermining themselves; for male-group dynamics include teasing and insults as bonding behavior. Too much of either weakens characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make conformity vs nonconformity meaningful
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters who automatically match the group's dynamic appear charismatic; those who don't conform read as outcasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately decide whether a character is a chameleon (adapts to group norms) or an outlier. Use conformity to show social skill and nonconformity to highlight isolation or principled difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid simply swapping gender roles in worldbuilding (matriarchy pitfall)
rubrics_metrics.description: When portraying a matriarchy, don't just put women in all roles of a patriarchy; consider different communication norms and socialization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write a matriarchy that communicates in more 'female fashion' (as per Genderlect insights) rather than merely replacing male characters with female ones. Use the prompt: write a scene set among a matriarchy and explore genuine differences in interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exceptions and neurodiversity to add interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples like a high-functioning autistic son show that neuroatypicality produces different conversational preferences (explicit vs implicit cues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate neurodiversity and individual variation to complicate gendered expectations—these exceptions can create conflict and depth and should be used intentionally.
